topics.title: Batteries & Power: Selection, Budgeting and Electrical Safety for Antweights
topics.scope_note: Covers LiPo/LiHV/Li-ion/LiFePO4/NiMH battery chemistry, cell-count and capacity selection, C-rating reality, voltage sag, power budgeting, charging practice, and electrical/mounting safety for 1 lb antweight and plastic antweight combat robots.

topics.title: Design Math: The 1 lb Antweight Engineering Toolkit
topics.scope_note: The complete engineering-math reference for designing a 1 lb (454 g) antweight combat robot: rotational dynamics and weapon inertia, gyroscopic effects, drivetrain and traction, electrical motor/battery sizing, structural impact and armor, weight/CG budgeting, and weapon bite geometry. Every formula carries a fully-worked numeric example using realistic antweight-scale values so an LLM (or a builder) can plug in their own numbers and compute a real answer.

topics.title: Drive Motors & Drivetrain Sizing
topics.scope_note: Drive motors, gearboxes, wheels, hubs, and drivetrain sizing for 1 lb antweight and plastic antweight combat robots, covering FingerTech, Repeat Robotics, N-series, Pololu, and brushless options plus the physics formulas used to size a drivetrain.

topics.title: Plastic Antweight (1 lb All-Plastic) Combat Robots
topics.scope_note: Complete reference for the 1 lb / 454 g all-plastic antweight combat robot class: exact ruleset wording and org-to-org variation on allowed/banned materials and metal exemptions, why the class exists, the dominant weapon/drive archetypes and why the plastic-only rule reshapes the meta, concrete build specs with per-part weight budgets, 3D printing material/settings/design-pattern practice, and where the community shares open-source designs.

topics.title: Weapon Motors: Selection & Sizing for Antweights
topics.scope_note: How to pick and size a spinning-weapon motor for 1 lb antweight and plastic antweight combat robots, using the FPV-drone brushless motor size ladder (11xx-28xx). Covers KV selection, motor constants, drivetrain layout (direct/belt/gear), spin-up time, thermal and mechanical failure modes, mounting, and worked numeric examples.

topics.title: Weight Classes, Rulesets & Safety Regulations
topics.scope_note: Covers the full combat-robotics weight class ladder (fairyweight through heavyweight), the major rulesets that govern competitions (SPARC, NHRL, RoboGames, BattleBots, AWS/UK, European/Australian variants), weight bonuses for walkers and multibots, banned weapons and materials, safety and inspection requirements, and match/judging rules. Every judgement is biased toward 1 lb antweight and plastic antweight, the classes most builders start in.

entities.name: Tattu 300mAh 2S 45C LiPo
entities.summary: A very common micro LiPo pack used in antweights and micro FPV, sized to fit inside the tightest 1 lb chassis while still driving a small brushless weapon and a pair of brushed drive motors.

entities.name: Tattu 300mAh 2S 75C LiHV
entities.summary: LiHV version of Tattu's popular 300mAh micro pack, charged to 4.35V/cell (7.6V nominal, 8.7V full) instead of the standard 4.2V/cell, giving roughly 4-8% more usable energy in the same size and weight.

entities.name: GNB LiHV 2S 300mAh 60C
entities.summary: Gaoneng (GNB) LiHV micro pack sold specifically as an antweight combat battery by hobby retailers; charges to 4.35V/cell for extra punch in the same 2S micro-pack footprint.

entities.name: GNB LiHV 4S 350mAh 70C
entities.summary: A 4S LiHV micro pack from Gaoneng, appropriate for higher-voltage antweight or light plastic-antweight drivetrains and higher-KV weapon setups that want 4S punch without the weight of a full-size 4S standard LiPo.

entities.name: GNB 1S 450mAh 4.35V HV
entities.summary: Single-cell LiHV pack, too low-voltage to run most antweight drivetrains alone but a real-world example of the small HV cells sometimes used to power an isolated receiver, telemetry, or a low-voltage weapon controller board in a combat robot's electronics bay.

entities.name: CNHL MiniStar 3S 450mAh 70C
entities.summary: A compact 3S 450mAh pack from CNHL (China Hobby Line) with an XT30 connector — a very typical capacity/voltage combination for an antweight or light plastic-antweight running a mid-KV brushless spinner plus two brushed drive motors.

entities.name: CNHL LiHV MiniStar 3S 450mAh 70C
entities.summary: LiHV sibling of the CNHL MiniStar 3S 450mAh pack, charged to 4.35V/cell (11.4V nominal vs 11.1V standard) for extra energy in the same physical package — a direct example of the real-world capacity gain LiHV offers antweight builders.

entities.name: Palm Power 2S 300mAh 65C (Gen2)
entities.summary: House-brand antweight LiPo sold directly by Palm Beach Bots, a US combat robotics vendor, with a JST connector and a separate balance lead — a pack designed and sold specifically for the antweight community rather than repurposed from FPV.

entities.name: Palm Power 3S 450mAh 45C (Gen2)
entities.summary: 3S 450mAh combat-specific pack from Palm Beach Bots with an XT30 connector, a common upgrade path from a 2S 300mAh pack once a builder moves to a higher-voltage brushless weapon.

entities.name: FingerTech Galaxy 2S LiPoly Pack
entities.summary: FingerTech Robotics' house line of small LiPo packs sold in multiple capacities for antweight and beetleweight kits such as the Viper V3; a long-running, combat-specific option predating the recent wave of Chinese FPV-brand crossover packs.

entities.name: Gens Ace 2S 300mAh 45C (typical)
entities.summary: Gens Ace is Tattu's sister brand under the same parent manufacturer (Grepow group) and sells directly comparable micro 2S/3S packs; a 300mAh 2S 45C pack in this line is a realistic, commonly-seen antweight-size option.

entities.name: Lumenier 2S 300mAh (micro FPV crossover)
entities.summary: Lumenier is primarily an FPV racing-drone battery brand; its micro 1S-2S packs are occasionally repurposed by antweight builders for the same reason Tattu/CNHL micro packs are — the size class overlaps almost exactly with what a 1 lb combat robot needs.

entities.name: RDQ Series 3S 450mAh (small format)
entities.summary: RaceDayQuads' in-house RDQ Series battery line spans micro FPV sizes up through 6S packs; a small 3S 450mAh option in this line is representative of the budget/value house-brand packs antweight builders sometimes substitute for name-brand Tattu/CNHL cells.

entities.name: Turnigy Nano-Tech 2S 300mAh
entities.summary: Turnigy's Nano-Tech line is a long-standing budget/value LiPo option sold through HobbyKing and resellers; still referenced as an entry-level combat robot battery choice, though less common today than dedicated combat-market brands.

entities.name: Molicel INR18650-P28A (Li-ion, context)
entities.summary: A high-drain 18650 cylindrical Li-ion cell, used here as the reference point for Li-ion in combat robotics: much higher capacity-per-cell and better cycle life than a LiPo pouch cell, but lower cell voltage (3.6-3.7V nominal vs 3.7V LiPo, similar) and a hard steel/nickel can that adds weight relative to energy density, plus a lower safe continuous discharge current per gram than a hot LiPo pouch.

entities.name: 2S LiFePO4 Receiver/Backup Pack
entities.summary: A small 2-cell LiFePO4 ("LiFe") pack at 6.6V nominal (3.3V/cell), the classic RC receiver-pack chemistry: much flatter discharge curve and far more abuse-tolerant than LiPo, occasionally used by antweight builders to power an isolated receiver or weapon-control board so it never browns out even if the main LiPo sags hard under weapon load.

entities.name: NiMH Stick Pack (legacy antweight power)
entities.summary: Nickel-metal-hydride packs were the default antweight power source in the earliest days of the class (roughly the 1990s through mid-2000s, before LiPo became affordable and reliable), typically a 6-cell 7.2V stick pack. Almost entirely obsolete today because LiPo offers 2-3x the energy density and can supply far higher current for its weight.

entities.name: ISDT 608AC Balance Charger
entities.summary: Compact 8A/200W AC/DC balance charger for 1-6S LiPo, LiHV, Li-ion, LiFe, NiMH and Pb packs with a detachable power supply and an XT60 charge port — a common choice among antweight builders for its small size and multi-chemistry support.

entities.name: HOTA D6 Pro Charger
entities.summary: A well-regarded 200W AC hobby balance charger for 1-6S packs with up to 1.6A per-cell balance current, popular in FPV and increasingly seen in antweight pits for its accuracy and fast balancing on small packs.

entities.name: SkyRC T1000 Charger
entities.summary: A 1-6S LiPo/LiHV balance charger and discharger from SkyRC, one of the long-established hobby charger brands; used by antweight builders both to charge match packs and to discharge them to storage voltage after an event.

entities.name: JST-PH 2.0mm Connector
entities.summary: A small 2.0mm-pitch connector rated for only a few amps continuous, standard on 1S-2S micro LiPo/LiHV packs; used throughout antweight electronics for battery main leads on the smallest packs and almost universally for balance leads on any pack size.

entities.name: XT30 Connector
entities.summary: A compact bullet-style connector rated for roughly 15-30A continuous depending on source and wire gauge, the standard 'step up' connector from tiny JST leads once an antweight's 3S or 4S pack needs to support real weapon current.

entities.name: C Rating
entities.summary: A LiPo battery's discharge capability expressed as a multiple of its own capacity per hour -- a 300 mAh pack rated 60C can (by the label) sustain 60 x 0.3 A = 18 A continuously. Real sustained performance is often lower than the printed rating suggests.

entities.name: Voltage Sag
entities.summary: The temporary drop in a battery's output voltage under load, caused by the pack's internal resistance; the higher the current draw and the higher the internal resistance, the larger the sag, and severe sag can drop system voltage below what the ESC or receiver needs to keep operating.

entities.name: LiHV (High-Voltage LiPo)
entities.summary: A LiPo cell chemistry variant built to be charged safely to 4.35V per cell instead of the standard 4.20V, giving roughly 5-10% more stored energy in the same physical cell at the cost of slightly reduced cycle life and the requirement for an LiHV-aware charger.

entities.name: Balance Charging
entities.summary: Charging method that monitors and tops off each individual cell in a multi-cell pack through its balance lead, so no single cell is overcharged or left behind, which is what keeps a multi-cell LiPo/LiHV pack safe and its cells even over many cycles.

entities.name: Storage Voltage
entities.summary: The recommended per-cell voltage (about 3.8V/cell, roughly 3.7-3.85V) at which a LiPo/LiHV pack should be kept for any period longer than a few days, chosen to minimize chemical stress on the cell compared to storing it fully charged or fully depleted.

entities.name: Brownout
entities.summary: A drop in supply voltage severe enough to cause a receiver, flight/weapon controller, or ESC to reset or behave erratically without fully losing power; in a 1 lb combat robot this is most often triggered by weapon-motor spin-up current sagging the shared main battery voltage below the electronics' minimum operating threshold.

entities.name: Internal Resistance
entities.summary: The effective resistance inside a battery pack (cell chemistry plus connections) that causes its terminal voltage to drop under load; internal resistance rises with cell age, cycle count, cold temperature and physical damage, which is why an older or damaged pack sags far more than a fresh one of the same rated C rating.

entities.name: Puffed Pack
entities.summary: A LiPo/LiHV pack whose pouch has visibly swollen from internal gas generation, a sign of degraded or damaged cell chemistry; a puffed pack should be retired immediately, never charged or discharged normally, and disposed of separately from healthy batteries.

entities.name: Pack Energy (Watt-hours)
entities.summary: Converts a pack's mAh capacity and nominal voltage into total stored energy in watt-hours, the unit that lets you compare packs of different cell counts and capacities on equal footing.

entities.name: Continuous / Burst Current from Capacity and C Rating
entities.summary: The standard way manufacturers express a pack's maximum discharge current, and the calculation an antweight builder should run backward — from an estimated real current draw — to check whether a candidate pack's C rating is remotely credible.

entities.name: Voltage Sag from Internal Resistance
entities.summary: Estimates how far pack voltage will drop under a given current draw using the pack's internal resistance, the direct cause-and-effect behind weapon-spin-up brownouts in small combat robots.

entities.name: Match Runtime from Average Current Draw
entities.summary: Estimates how long a pack will last in a match given an average (not peak) current draw across drive and weapon combined, used to size capacity against the standard 3-minute combat robotics match length.

entities.name: Total System Current Draw (Drive + Weapon)
entities.summary: Builds a rough total current budget for an antweight by summing estimated drive-motor stall/running current and weapon-motor running current, the starting point for both C-rating and capacity sizing.

entities.name: Angular velocity from RPM
entities.summary: Converts a motor or weapon speed given in RPM (revolutions per minute) into angular velocity in radians per second, the unit every rotational-KE and torque formula on this page needs.

entities.name: Moment of inertia — solid disc / cylinder about its central axis
entities.summary: MOI of a uniform solid disc (or short solid cylinder) spinning about the axis through its own center, perpendicular to its face. This is the base case for most vertical-spinner and drum weapon discs.

entities.name: Moment of inertia — annulus (ring with a hole, e.g. a hub or drum wall)
entities.summary: MOI of a flat ring-shaped mass with both an outer and inner radius (a washer shape), such as a weapon disc with a large center bore, or a drum's cylindrical wall seen end-on.

entities.name: Moment of inertia — thin ring / hoop (all mass at one radius)
entities.summary: MOI of a thin hoop or ring where essentially all the mass sits at a single radius, such as a steel reinforcement band shrunk onto the rim of a disc weapon.

entities.name: Moment of inertia — slender rod about its own center (horizontal bar spinner)
entities.summary: MOI of a uniform straight bar rotating about an axis through its own midpoint, perpendicular to its length. This is the standard model for a horizontal (full-width) bar spinner weapon.

entities.name: Moment of inertia — slender rod about one end (hammer / axe / flail arm)
entities.summary: MOI of a uniform straight arm rotating about a pivot at one of its own ends, rather than its center — the correct model for a hammer, axe, or single-pivot flail arm.

entities.name: Moment of inertia — point mass at a radius
entities.summary: MOI of a small, compact mass treated as concentrated at a single point, a distance r from the rotation axis. Used for bolts, counterweights, or small hard-faced tips whose own size is negligible next to their distance from the axis.

entities.name: Moment of inertia — thin-walled cylinder / tube about its long axis
entities.summary: MOI of a thin cylindrical shell (a tube or drum's outer wall) spinning about its own central longitudinal axis. Mathematically identical in form to the thin-ring case (all wall mass sits at radius r regardless of the tube's length), and is the right model for a hollow drum-spinner shell or a shaft/hub.

entities.name: Parallel axis theorem — combining a compound weapon's parts into one total MOI
entities.summary: The general rule for adding up the MOI of a multi-part weapon (a disc plus a bolted-on tooth, a hub plus inserts, etc.): each part's own MOI about its own center of mass, plus that part's mass times the square of how far its center of mass sits from the actual rotation axis. Summing this over every part gives the true total MOI used in every KE/tip-speed/spin-up calculation.

entities.name: Rotational kinetic energy stored in a spinning weapon
entities.summary: The total kinetic energy stored in the weapon at a given spin speed -- the number combat robotics people mean when they say a weapon 'has X joules'.

entities.name: Tip speed of a spinning weapon
entities.summary: The linear (straight-line) speed of the outermost point of the weapon -- the speed at which the tooth or blade edge is actually moving through the air, which is what does the cutting/hitting.

entities.name: Effective (reduced) mass of a spinning weapon at its tooth
entities.summary: Converts a rotating weapon's inertia into an equivalent straight-line mass, as felt at one specific radius (usually the tooth/tip). This lets you treat a weapon hit like a simple linear collision: KE = 0.5 * m_eff * v_tip^2 gives the same energy as the rotational formula.

entities.name: Momentum transfer to the opponent on impact
entities.summary: Models a weapon strike as a partially-inelastic collision between the weapon's effective mass (at the tip) and the opponent's total mass, to estimate how fast the opponent gets thrown/launched. Coefficient of restitution e is empirical: roughly 0.2-0.3 for a mostly-absorbed/deforming hit, 0.4-0.5 for a stiffer, more elastic bounce-off hit.

entities.name: Spin-up time from motor torque and weapon MOI
entities.summary: Estimates how long a weapon takes to reach operating speed from a standstill, using the average available motor torque over the acceleration and the weapon's total MOI. Long spin-up times are a real tactical liability (weapon is weak/inert while re-spinning after a hit).

entities.name: Energy actually delivered in one hit, vs total energy stored
entities.summary: A weapon rarely dumps its entire stored KE into a single hit -- the disc only slows down by however much the impact actually resists it, and keeps most of its spin for the next hit. This computes the energy actually delivered from the RPM drop observed/expected during a strike.

entities.name: Gyroscopic precession torque from turning while the weapon spins
entities.summary: When a chassis carrying a spinning weapon is itself rotated (yawed) by the drivetrain, gyroscopic precession produces a reaction torque trying to tip the chassis about a THIRD axis, perpendicular to both the weapon's spin axis and the turn axis. This is the physics behind vertical-spinner 'gyro dance'.

entities.name: Tipping-moment threshold for a 1 lb chassis
entities.summary: A first-order estimate of how much overturning moment a lightweight chassis can resist before it starts to lift/rock about the edge of its wheel track, using just weight and half the track width. It ignores CG height (a more complete model also uses formula-cg-tipping-angle), but is a fast way to check a precession torque against a real robot.

entities.name: Predicting the maximum safe turn rate before gyro-dance tipping
entities.summary: Rearranges the precession-torque and tipping-moment formulas to solve directly for the fastest a driver can yaw the chassis (at a given weapon speed) before the precession reaction exceeds the tipping threshold and the robot starts to rock.

entities.name: Top speed from motor RPM, gear ratio, and wheel diameter
entities.summary: Converts a drive motor's raw (ungeared) no-load RPM through the gearbox ratio and wheel size into the robot's theoretical top ground speed.

entities.name: Acceleration from motor torque (torque-limited case)
entities.summary: Converts drive-motor output torque, through the gearbox and wheel radius, into a forward driving force, and from there into acceleration -- BEFORE checking whether the wheels can actually put that much force onto the arena floor (see formula-traction-limited-force, which usually governs instead for lightweight antweights).

entities.name: Traction-limited pushing/driving force
entities.summary: The maximum forward (or pushing) force a robot's drive wheels can transmit to the floor before they simply spin in place, set by the robot's weight on the wheels and the wheel-to-floor friction coefficient -- NOT by how much torque the motors can produce. For a 454 g robot this is almost always the true limiting factor, well below what the drivetrain can output.

entities.name: Wheel-slip threshold and the resulting real acceleration
entities.summary: Compares the torque-limited drive force against the traction-limited force to determine which one actually governs, then computes the robot's real (traction-limited) acceleration -- the number that matters for a 1 lb robot, which is almost always far below the torque-limited number.

entities.name: Torque and traction required to climb an opponent's wedge
entities.summary: Two separate conditions must both hold to drive up onto an opponent's wedge at angle theta: (1) the drivetrain must supply enough torque at the wheel, and (2) the wheels must have enough traction against the now-tilted (and often slippery) wedge surface -- whichever is smaller sets the actual climbable angle.

entities.name: Mechanical power delivered at a given speed
entities.summary: Basic power = force x velocity relationship, used to check how much continuous power the drivetrain is actually asking of the battery/ESC at cruising speed versus during a hard push.

entities.name: Torque constant Kt from velocity constant Kv (exact form AND common hobby shorthand)
entities.summary: Kv (rpm per volt of back-EMF) and Kt (torque per amp) describe the same physical motor constant in different units. The EXACT, physically-derived relation is Kt[N*m/A] = 60 / (2*pi*Kv[rpm/V]) = 9.5493 / Kv. The widely-used HOBBY SHORTHAND Kt = 8.27 / Kv is NOT the same physical law -- it silently bakes in an assumed ~87% mechanical/electrical efficiency (8.27/9.5493 = 0.866), so it already includes a loss derating. Use the exact 9.5493 form for real torque/spin-up physics, and only use 8.27 if you specifically want a quick 'expected real-world output torque' guess and are not also applying a separate efficiency factor on top of it.

entities.name: Stall torque from Kt and stall current
entities.summary: The maximum torque a motor can produce, occurring at zero RPM (locked rotor) when the full stall current flows.

entities.name: Stall current from voltage and winding resistance
entities.summary: The current a motor draws when its rotor is locked (RPM = 0), limited only by the winding resistance since there is no back-EMF at zero speed. This is the highest current the motor (and its ESC) will ever be asked to pass.

entities.name: No-load RPM from Kv and voltage
entities.summary: The speed a motor spins at with no mechanical load and no current-draw losses -- an idealized upper bound. Real no-load speed under actual bearing/brush/air-drag friction is slightly lower than this.

entities.name: DC motor power curve and peak power at half stall speed
entities.summary: For an ideal DC (brushed or BLDC-as-DC-equivalent) motor, torque falls off linearly with speed from T_stall at 0 rpm to 0 at no-load rpm. Multiplying torque by speed gives a power curve that peaks exactly halfway between (at half the no-load speed and half the stall torque), which is the operating point a weapon or drivetrain wants to sit near for maximum mechanical power.

entities.name: ESC current headroom / derating
entities.summary: An ESC's continuous-current rating should be sized well above the motor's realistic stall current, since brief stalls (weapon impacts, drivetrain jams against a wall) are normal in combat and are exactly when full stall current flows.

entities.name: Battery C-rating to continuous amps
entities.summary: Converts a LiPo pack's C-rating (a multiple of its own capacity) into an actual continuous-current figure in amps, the number that needs to be compared against total robot current draw.

entities.name: Battery energy capacity in watt-hours
entities.summary: Converts a battery's amp-hour capacity and nominal voltage into total stored energy in watt-hours, useful for comparing packs across different cell counts (voltages) on an equal-energy basis.

entities.name: Voltage sag from internal resistance under load
entities.summary: The battery's terminal voltage drops below its nominal/open-circuit voltage in proportion to the current drawn and the pack's internal resistance. Underestimating this leads to overestimating available torque/power right when it's needed most (weapon stall, hard push).

entities.name: Motor efficiency estimate at an operating point
entities.summary: Ratio of useful mechanical power out to electrical power in, at a specific torque/speed operating point -- NOT a constant, it varies across the motor's speed range and is generally best near (but not exactly at) the peak-power point.

entities.name: Impact force from momentum change and contact time
entities.summary: The average force during an impact equals the momentum change divided by how long the impact takes -- the key reason very brief, stiff impacts produce enormous peak forces compared to the same momentum change spread over a longer contact time (see formula-compliance-reduces-peak-force).

entities.name: Basic stress from force and area
entities.summary: The foundational stress equation, used to check whether an impact force is survivable for a given material and contact-patch size, by comparing the resulting stress to the material's yield strength.

entities.name: Beam bending stress in a flat armor panel
entities.summary: Models an armor panel bolted at two edges as a simply-supported beam under a central point impact load, giving the peak bending stress at the panel's surface -- the standard first check for whether a given armor thickness/material will survive a hit without cracking or permanently bending.

entities.name: Why compliance (a longer stopping time) reduces peak impact force
entities.summary: For the same momentum change, spreading the impact over a longer contact time (via a compliant mount, standoff, or slightly flexible armor) directly and proportionally lowers the peak force -- the physical reason 'a little give' in a mount often survives hits that a rigid one cracks under.

entities.name: Bolt shear stress estimate
entities.summary: Estimates the shear stress carried by a group of bolts resisting a reaction force (e.g. a weapon-motor mount reacting the impact force), by spreading the force evenly across the bolts' shear cross-sectional area.

entities.name: Weight budget allocation across subsystems
entities.summary: Splits the robot's total weight limit into subsystem budgets by percentage, the first step of any antweight design before a single part is chosen. Typical splits differ sharply between a metal-weapon spinner and a plastic-antweight build (see the two worked-walkthrough chunks).

entities.name: Tipping angle from CG height and track/wheelbase
entities.summary: The lateral (or fore-aft) tilt angle at which a robot's center of gravity passes directly over its wheel contact line and it starts to roll over -- a low, wide robot with a low CG resists tipping far better than a tall, narrow one, which matters both for wedge rammer defense and for the gyro-dance check above.

entities.name: Approximate self-righting condition for a rounded-shell design
entities.summary: A simplified rule of thumb for shell/dome-shaped robots (common on shell spinners and some invertible bots): if the robot's center-of-gravity height stays below the radius of its rounded shell, gravity alone tends to roll it back onto its wheels when flipped, rather than leaving it balanced or stuck upside-down.

entities.name: Sheet/panel weight from area, thickness, and material density
entities.summary: Basic mass-from-volume-and-density calculation, used constantly when picking armor or frame stock thickness against the weight budget.

entities.name: Bite depth from closing speed, weapon RPM, and tooth count
entities.summary: How far (in material depth) a spinning weapon's tooth advances into an opponent between successive tooth strikes, given how fast the two robots are closing together. Fewer teeth at the same RPM means a LONGER gap between hits, so each hit gets a deeper 'bite' -- the core reason single-tooth vertical spinners are favored for maximum per-hit penetration over multi-tooth designs.

entities.name: Hit frequency from RPM and tooth count
entities.summary: How many times per second a spinning weapon's tooth (or teeth) strike, used both for the bite-depth formula above and for estimating cumulative impact loading on the weapon mount and motor over a fight.

entities.name: Kv (velocity constant)
entities.summary: A motor's Kv rating describes how many RPM it would spin per volt applied, with no load and no back-EMF losses considered. Higher Kv motors spin faster but produce less torque per amp for a given size/winding.

entities.name: Kt (torque constant)
entities.summary: A motor's Kt rating describes how much torque it produces per amp of current. The physically exact relation to Kv is Kt[N*m/A] = 9.5493/Kv[rpm/V]; a widely-used hobby shorthand, Kt = 8.27/Kv, bakes in an assumed ~87% efficiency and gives a lower number than the exact form. See formula-kt-from-kv.

entities.name: Moment of inertia (MOI)
entities.summary: A measure of how a mass's distribution around a rotation axis resists angular acceleration -- the rotational equivalent of mass. Depends strongly on how far mass sits from the spin axis (radius squared), which is why small changes in weapon radius have an outsized effect on stored energy.

entities.name: Radius of gyration
entities.summary: The distance from the rotation axis at which the weapon's entire mass could be concentrated as a single point and produce the same moment of inertia. Useful as a single number summarizing how spread-out (vs concentrated) a weapon's mass distribution is.

entities.name: Gyroscopic precession
entities.summary: The tendency of a spinning object's rotation axis to react to an applied torque by tilting perpendicular to both the spin axis and the applied torque, rather than in the direction naively expected. In vertical spinners, turning the chassis while the weapon is spinning applies exactly this kind of torque, producing an unwanted tipping reaction.

entities.name: Tip speed
entities.summary: The linear speed of the outermost point of a rotating weapon, calculated as RPM x diameter x 0.00436 to get feet/second (the formula SPARC uses for its slow-spinner and open-air-combat speed limits); a key design variable because plastic weapons have a much lower survivable tip speed than metal ones before they self-destruct.

entities.name: Stall current
entities.summary: The current a motor draws when its rotor is fully locked (zero RPM), limited only by winding resistance. This is the highest current the motor and its ESC will ever see, and is the number ESC/wire/connector sizing should be checked against.

entities.name: Stall torque
entities.summary: The maximum torque a motor can produce, occurring at zero RPM when the full stall current flows.

entities.name: No-load speed
entities.summary: The RPM a motor spins at with no mechanical load applied, close to (but slightly above) its real free-spinning speed once bearing drag and air resistance are accounted for.

entities.name: ESC (Electronic Speed Controller)
entities.summary: The electronic module that takes a control signal and battery power and drives a motor (brushed or brushless) at a commanded speed/direction. Antweights use one ESC per drive motor plus a separate ESC for the weapon motor, each sized with current headroom above the motor's stall current.

entities.name: Gear ratio
entities.summary: The reduction between a motor's own shaft speed and its output shaft speed after a gearbox, expressed as motor-turns-per-output-turn (e.g. 20:1 means the output turns once for every 20 motor turns, at 1/20th the RPM but roughly 20x the torque, efficiency losses aside).

entities.name: Bite depth
entities.summary: How far into an opponent's material a spinning weapon's tooth penetrates before the next tooth (or the same tooth on its next revolution) arrives -- governed by closing speed, weapon RPM, and tooth count.

entities.name: Effective (reduced) mass
entities.summary: A way of re-expressing a rotating weapon's inertia as an equivalent straight-line mass at a chosen reference radius (usually the tooth tip), so that ordinary linear collision/impact formulas can be applied directly.

entities.name: Spin-up time
entities.summary: How long a weapon takes to reach its operating speed from rest (or from a partial-speed dip after a hit), set by the available average motor torque and the weapon's total moment of inertia. A liability when too long, since the weapon is weak while re-spinning.

entities.name: Traction-limited (vs torque-limited)
entities.summary: Describes a drivetrain whose real-world acceleration/pushing force is set by how much force the wheels can transmit to the floor (weight x friction coefficient) rather than by how much torque the motors can produce -- the normal condition for lightweight (1 lb class) combat robots.

entities.name: Parallel axis theorem
entities.summary: The rule for computing a part's moment of inertia about an axis other than its own center of mass: add the mass times the square of the offset distance to the part's own center-of-mass MOI. Used to combine a multi-part weapon (disc plus bolted-on tooth, etc.) into one total MOI.

entities.name: Compliance (structural)
entities.summary: Deliberate flexibility or give in a mount, standoff, or panel that extends the time over which an impact decelerates a part, which lowers the peak force for the same momentum change -- a key reason 'slightly soft' mounts often survive hits that fully rigid ones crack under.

entities.name: Center of gravity (CG)
entities.summary: The single point at which a robot's entire weight can be considered to act. Its height above the ground and its position relative to the wheelbase/track strongly influence tipping resistance, wedge performance, and self-righting behavior.

entities.name: Tipping angle
entities.summary: The angle of tilt at which a robot's center of gravity passes directly over its wheel (or shell) contact line and it begins to roll over, set by CG height relative to track width or wheelbase.

entities.name: FingerTech "Silver Spark" 16mm Gearmotor
entities.summary: The default drive gearmotor for 1 lb antweight robots: a Mabuchi FK-050 brushed motor mated to an all-metal 16mm spur gearhead, sold across a ladder of 9 gear ratios from 11.1:1 (fast) to 600:1 (slow/high-torque).

entities.name: FingerTech Silver Spark 16mm Gearmotor, 11.1:1
entities.summary: The fastest stock Silver Spark ratio, used when a builder wants maximum top speed and dodge/reposition ability rather than pushing torque, typically paired with a larger (~2in) wheel.

entities.name: FingerTech Silver Spark 16mm Gearmotor, 100:1
entities.summary: A mid-high torque Silver Spark ratio popular on control bots and lifters that need strong pushing/lifting force more than raw speed.

entities.name: FingerTech Silver Spark 16mm Gearmotor, 200:1
entities.summary: One of the highest stock-ratio Silver Sparks, used for slow, high-torque applications like weapon lifters, self-righters, or extremely traction-limited pushing bots rather than main drive.

entities.name: FingerTech "Gold Spark" 16mm Gearmotor
entities.summary: FingerTech's budget-tier 16mm gearmotor: the same Mabuchi FK-050 base motor as the Silver Spark but with a plastic (not all-metal) gear stage, sold in 8 ratios from 20:1 to 360:1. Positioned for hobby/mini-sumo/line-following use and lighter-duty antweight builds rather than front-line competitive drive.

entities.name: FingerTech Gold Spark 16mm Gearmotor, 150:1
entities.summary: A higher-torque Gold Spark ratio near the top of its safe operating range before hitting the plastic output gear's 6.84 kg-cm damage threshold.

entities.name: FingerTech "MegaSpark" Brushless 24mm Planetary Gearmotor
entities.summary: A premium 24mm brushless planetary gearmotor sold through the FingerTech ecosystem (via resellers), sized more for beetleweight than antweight but relevant as the high-end brushless benchmark antweight brushless pods are compared against.

entities.name: Repeat Robotics "Mini Brushed" Mk2 Antweight Gearmotor
entities.summary: Repeat Robotics' antweight brushed planetary gearmotor, positioned as a more durable alternative to spur-gear motors like Silver Spark, using a multi-stage all-metal planetary gearbox for higher torque density and durability.

entities.name: Repeat Robotics "Mini" Brushless 1106 Mk4.1 Gearmotor
entities.summary: Repeat Robotics' flagship antweight brushless drive gearmotor: a custom-wound 1106 outrunner brushless motor built directly into a 2-stage, 28.5:1, all-metal 16mm planetary gearbox with a 4mm hardened output shaft, aimed at builders who want more speed and efficiency than brushed Silver Sparks at a similar weight.

entities.name: Repeat Robotics "Mini Pro" 1106 Gearmotor
entities.summary: A higher-spec / higher-price variant of Repeat's 1106 brushless antweight drive gearmotor line, sold alongside the standard Mk4.1 for builders wanting extra performance or refinement (e.g. better bearings, tighter tolerances).

entities.name: Repeat Robotics Compact Brushless 1806 Drive Gearmotor
entities.summary: A lightweight brushless planetary gearmotor built around an 1806-size motor, marketed as the lightest brushless beetleweight drive motor on the market; included here as context for scaling brushless drive up from antweight, or for extra-light plastic-antweight-adjacent builds where a lower part count matters more than absolute minimum weight.

entities.name: Generic N20 Gearmotor, 6V, 100:1
entities.summary: A widely sold 12mm-diameter micro DC gearmotor (compatible with Sanyo NA4S-style gearboxes) used by budget and plastic-antweight builders as a cheap alternative to FingerTech/Repeat/Pololu motors, at the cost of unit-to-unit quality consistency.

entities.name: Generic N20 Gearmotor, 6V, 298:1
entities.summary: A slow, high-torque N20 variant near the top of the common ratio ladder, used for lifters, self-righters, or very traction-limited plastic-antweight drives rather than fast main drive.

entities.name: Generic N20 Gearmotor, 12V, 1000:1
entities.summary: The slowest, highest-torque stock N20 ratio; the 1000:1 (and 380:1) versions get a slightly longer, reinforced gearbox and a higher torque rating than the rest of the line, making them the ones most likely to survive at this extreme reduction.

entities.name: Generic N30 Gearmotor, 6V, 50:1
entities.summary: The larger sibling of the N20, using a bigger-diameter motor can (~30mm class) for more torque and current handling at the cost of extra weight; used in antweights (not usually plastic antweights, where every gram counts more) when N20 torque isn't enough but a 16mm FingerTech-class motor is still preferred to save weight.

entities.name: Generic N10 Gearmotor, 6V, 100:1
entities.summary: The smallest of the common N-series (N10/N20/N30) gearmotor family, used in fairyweight robots and the very lightest plastic antweight builds where every gram matters more than raw torque.

entities.name: Pololu Micro Metal Gearmotor HP 6V, 30:1
entities.summary: Pololu's High-Power (HP) tune of its popular micro metal gearmotor line at a fast 30:1 ratio: a 10x12mm all-metal gearbox on a 3mm D-shaft output, favoring speed and current draw over the LP/MP tunes of the same physical motor.

entities.name: Pololu Micro Metal Gearmotor MP 6V, 30:1
entities.summary: The Medium-Power (MP) tune of Pololu's micro metal gearmotor, splitting the difference between the low-current LP and high-current HP versions of the same physical gearbox and ratio.

entities.name: Pololu Micro Metal Gearmotor LP 6V, 50:1
entities.summary: The Low-Power (LP) tune of Pololu's micro metal gearmotor, drawing the least current of the three power tunes for a given ratio — useful when a builder is current-budget constrained (e.g. a very small ESC or shared receiver battery).

entities.name: Pololu Micro Metal Gearmotor HP 6V, 100:1
entities.summary: A commonly chosen ratio/power combination for antweight-scale robots wanting a precision-made alternative to generic N20 motors, balancing speed and torque for typical 1.5-2in wheels.

entities.name: Pololu Micro Metal Gearmotor, Extended Motor Shaft variant
entities.summary: A version of the micro metal gearmotor line with the motor's rear shaft extended through the back of the case, letting a builder mount an encoder disc, a second small pulley, or a cooling/inertia element on the motor's non-gearbox end without modifying the motor.

entities.name: 1104-size Brushless Motor (FPV-derived) for Custom Drive Pods
entities.summary: An 11mm-diameter, 4mm-tall outrunner brushless motor, originally developed for micro FPV drones, repurposed by combat robot builders into custom or off-the-shelf (e.g. Repeat Robotics) 16mm drive gearboxes for antweight main drive.

entities.name: 1404-size Brushless Motor (FPV-derived) for Custom Drive Pods
entities.summary: A 14mm-diameter, 4mm-tall outrunner brushless motor, larger-stator sibling of the 1104/1106 sizes, used in higher-power antweight or lighter beetleweight custom drive builds where more torque/current handling is wanted from a similarly slim motor.

entities.name: Modified Continuous-Rotation 9g Micro Servo (Drive)
entities.summary: A standard 9g hobby micro servo (e.g. SG90-class) with its position-limiting potentiometer removed or bypassed (replaced with a fixed voltage divider) so it spins continuously instead of to a commanded angle, letting the transmitter's stick position set speed and direction directly with zero external electronics.

entities.name: Stock Continuous-Rotation Micro Servo (FS90R-class)
entities.summary: A factory-built continuous-rotation micro servo (no user modification needed), functionally equivalent to a hand-modified 9g servo but sold ready to use, popular for beginner plastic antweight and fairyweight drive.

entities.name: 16mm Planetary Gearbox Module (generic/Repeat-style)
entities.summary: A multi-stage (typically 2-3 stage) all-metal planetary gearbox module in the same 16mm form factor popularized by FingerTech's spur-gear Spark line, used by Repeat Robotics and others to mate to brushed or brushless motors for higher torque density and durability than a comparable spur gearbox.

entities.name: N-Series (N10/N20/N30) Gearbox: Metal vs Plastic Gear Stages
entities.summary: A comparison entity describing the inconsistent internal construction of budget N-series gearmotors: many listings advertise "metal gear" but only some internal stages are actually metal, with the rest plastic, and quality varies not just by listing but by individual unit within the same order — the core of the antweight community's "quality lottery" problem with these motors.

entities.name: FingerTech Lite Flite Foam Wheel
entities.summary: FingerTech's neoprene foam wheel, the most widely used antweight wheel: extremely light, shock-absorbing, and surprisingly grippy for a plain foam tire, sold in a wide range of diameters and two widths to fit the Twist/Snap/Lite hub system.

entities.name: Silicone-Coated / Cast Silicone Tire
entities.summary: A foam or 3D-printed wheel core coated or wrapped in a thin layer of cast silicone rubber (Shore A ~20-50 durometer), a common DIY upgrade path when bare foam or bare plastic doesn't provide enough grip for a control bot or pushing match.

entities.name: 3D-Printed TPU Wheel
entities.summary: A wheel (tire, or tire+hub as one piece) 3D printed in flexible TPU filament (commonly 85-95A shore hardness), a zero-marginal-cost option extremely popular in plastic antweights since it fits the class's plastic-construction ethos and needs no purchased hub/tire hardware.

entities.name: O-Ring Tire Wheel
entities.summary: A lightweight wheel technique where a plain hub (aluminum, printed plastic, or Delrin) has a groove sized to hold a rubber O-ring (or several stacked), which is stretched onto the hub's outer diameter to act as a cheap, easily replaceable, grippy tire.

entities.name: Banebots T61 Compliant Wheel
entities.summary: A compliant (flexible tread) wheel line from Banebots that conforms to surfaces for extra grip and control, sold in 6 hardness options, 4 diameters, and 4 hub-shaft sizes, primarily sized for beetleweight/hobbyweight but with small diameters usable in heavier antweight or control-bot-focused builds; the smaller Banebots T40 line is aimed more directly at ant/fairy scale.

entities.name: FingerTech Lite Hub
entities.summary: FingerTech's lightest wheel hub, designed to mount common foam wheels onto a 3mm motor shaft with minimal added weight.

entities.name: FingerTech Snap Hub
entities.summary: An anodized 6061 aluminum hub from FingerTech that holds a foam tire tightly via a custom washer with a recess to prevent the retaining snap ring from coming loose, offering more strength than the plastic Lite Hub at a modest weight cost.

entities.name: FingerTech Twist Hub
entities.summary: An anodized 6061 aluminum hub secured to the motor shaft with an 8-32 setscrew, holding the foam tire tightly via a locking washer; sold in Thin (0.50in) and Wide (0.75in) widths for both 3mm and 4mm shafts.

entities.name: GT2 Belt & Pulley Drivetrain Set (antweight scale)
entities.summary: A small GT2 (2mm pitch) timing belt and matching aluminum or 3D-printed pulley set used to link a front and rear wheel on each side of a 4WD antweight, letting two motors drive four wheels instead of needing four separate drive motors.

entities.name: Robot Speed from Motor RPM and Wheel Diameter
entities.summary: Converts a drivetrain's output (wheel) RPM and wheel diameter into a theoretical no-load top speed, the first step in sizing any antweight drivetrain.

entities.name: Required Motor Torque for a Target Acceleration / Pushing Force
entities.summary: Sizes the motor-shaft stall torque needed to accelerate a given robot mass at a target rate (or to sustain a target pushing force), working back through the wheel radius, gear ratio, and gearbox efficiency.

entities.name: Traction Limit: Why Torque Beyond Available Grip Is Wasted
entities.summary: Defines the maximum pushing/accelerating force a drivetrain can actually put to the ground, set by wheel-to-floor friction rather than motor torque; any drivetrain torque capacity beyond this ceiling just spins the wheels and wastes battery/heat instead of producing more force.

entities.name: Stall Current vs ESC Rating and Duty-Cycle Thermal Limits
entities.summary: Explains how to size a drive ESC/driver's continuous and burst current ratings against a motor's stall current, and why sustained full-stall (e.g. pinned against a wall or opponent) is a thermal, time-limited event rather than something a small combat robot motor can hold indefinitely.

entities.name: Selecting a Gear Ratio from a Desired Top Speed
entities.summary: Rearranges the speed formula to solve for the gear ratio needed to hit a target top speed with a given motor and wheel diameter, then checks the result against the ratios actually available off the shelf.

entities.name: Plastic Antweight
entities.summary: A 1 lb (454 g) variant of antweight in which the entire robot (except electronics, motors, and fasteners) must be built from approved 3D-printable/thermoplastic materials. Started by Western Allied Robotics to make antweight building cheaper and more accessible, later folded into SPARC as an official weight-class variant. It is the fastest-growing beginner class because a full robot can be printed on a hobby FDM printer for well under $50.

entities.name: SPARC Plastic Class (Robot Construction Specifications v1.6, §16.3)
entities.summary: The template ruleset most North American plastic-ant events build from. Defines the class's spirit, the exact allowed plastics list (verified verbatim against the current v1.6 PDF, 21 September 2025), the COTS-parts exemption with explicit permitted/not-permitted examples, and a notably strict post-processing ban.

entities.name: SCAR 2025 Ruleset — Plastic Ant Weight Class
entities.summary: SoCal Attack Robots' 2025 ruleset section covering Plastic Ant, closely following SPARC's template but adding explicit weight bonuses for shufflers and non-wheeled locomotion and an explicit magnet/UHMW ban.

entities.name: SCAR Plastic Ant FAQ
entities.summary: A supplementary FAQ document SCAR publishes alongside its main ruleset that names specific approved filament brands and explicitly bans several materials (TPU, nylon, composites, epoxy coatings) that are ambiguous under the base ruleset's plain-language material list.

entities.name: Western Allied Robotics (WAR) Plastic Antweight — Original 2015 Rules
entities.summary: The founding ruleset of the plastic antweight class, introduced by Western Allied Robotics in 2015, restricting the chassis and weapon to PET/PETG/ABS/PLA/PLA+ while exempting motors, electronics, axles, fasteners and adhesives.

entities.name: Robot Ruckus Plastic Ant Construction Rules
entities.summary: Robot Ruckus's plastic ant rules, requiring 3D-printed PLA/PLA+/ABS/PETG construction and following the standard metal-fastener exemption, with an explicit requirement that surface screws be countersunk or shrouded so they cannot act as armor or weapon impactors.

entities.name: Plastic Ant Vertical Spinner
entities.summary: The single most common competitive plastic-ant archetype: a spinning disc or drum on a vertical (side-to-side relative to the arena floor, striking-face-forward) axis, printed from PETG or ABS, driven by a small brushless outrunner. Dominant because a thick printed disc keeps its weapon mass close to the axis and hits with blunt, ring-shaped force rather than requiring a hardened cutting edge.

entities.name: Plastic Ant Drum Spinner (Undercutter)
entities.summary: A full-width horizontal drum, usually printed in PETG for impact ductility, spun on an axis parallel to the ground and low to the floor to drive under opponents. The drum's wall thickness itself does the damage (blunt/ram) rather than teeth, and the wide printed cylinder is naturally stronger against delamination than a thin bar.

entities.name: Plastic Ant Horizontal (Bar) Spinner
entities.summary: A single spinning bar or blade on a vertical axis (spinning in the horizontal plane, striking outward in a circle), the dominant weapon type in metal antweight but a comparatively weak and fragile choice in plastic because the weapon tip itself must be printed plastic rather than hardened steel.

entities.name: Plastic Ant Beater Bar / Egg-beater
entities.summary: A low, wide horizontal weapon bar mounted close to the floor at the front of the robot that beats upward into an opponent's underside, similar in geometry to a drum spinner but usually a simpler bar rather than a full cylinder, printed thick to survive repeated low-clearance strikes.

entities.name: Plastic Ant Wedge / Control Bot
entities.summary: A weaponless or lightly-weaponed robot built around a low front wedge and strong drivetrain, designed to win on driving skill, ring-out and judges' decision rather than weapon damage — often the recommended first build and a strong beginner-friendly counter to fragile plastic spinners.

entities.name: Plastic Ant Lifter
entities.summary: A wedge-fronted robot with a servo- or small-motor-actuated arm that scoops and lifts an opponent to expose their underside or throw them, using printed linkages instead of the pneumatics common in bigger lifters.

entities.name: N20 Micro Gearmotor (6-12V)
entities.summary: A tiny brushed DC gearmotor in a roughly 12x10x10mm metal gearbox, the most common drive motor in plastic antweights due to its low cost, light weight, and wide range of stock gear ratios.

entities.name: 130-Size Brushed Drive Motor
entities.summary: A classic small brushed can motor (the same family used in cheap toy cars) sometimes paired with a 3D-printed or small stock gearbox for antweight drive; cheaper and more available than purpose-built combat drive motors.

entities.name: Micro Brushless Outrunner, ~2600KV (1811-size class)
entities.summary: A small brushless outrunner motor in the size class commonly used for antweight vertical spinner and drum weapons, run on 2S LiPo for a good balance of RPM and torque within a plastic ant's weight and tip-speed goals.

entities.name: Micro Brushless Outrunner, ~1400KV
entities.summary: A lower-kv small outrunner used for horizontal/bar spinners and drums where more torque and a lower tip speed (kinder to a printed weapon) is preferred over raw RPM.

entities.name: Micro Brushless Weapon ESC (~6A)
entities.summary: A tiny brushless ESC (often an AM32 or BLHeli-based FPV-drone-derived board) used to run the weapon motor in a plastic ant, valued for its very low weight relative to the alternative of a brushed weapon motor and controller.

entities.name: Micro Combo RX + Dual Brushed ESC Board
entities.summary: An all-in-one micro PCB combining a radio receiver with two small brushed motor drivers, the standard drive-electronics solution in antweights because it saves the weight and wiring of separate RX and ESC boards.

entities.name: 2S 300mAh LiPo Battery
entities.summary: A small 2-cell lithium polymer pack, the most common power source for plastic ant vertical spinner and drum builds, giving 7.4V nominal for both a brushless weapon motor and brushed drive motors.

entities.name: 1S 300-500mAh LiPo Battery
entities.summary: A single-cell LiPo pack used in budget or control-focused plastic ants running low-voltage brushed drive motors without a brushless weapon.

entities.name: Printed Hub + TPU Tire Wheel
entities.summary: A 3D-printed rigid hub (PLA+/PETG) with a separately printed TPU tire pressed or glued on, the standard plastic-ant wheel: fully print-and-replace, and legal everywhere since both hub and tire are on the approved plastic list (subject to local TPU rulings).

entities.name: COTS Foam/Silicone Antweight Wheel
entities.summary: An off-the-shelf foam or silicone-tired wheel (e.g. FingerTech, Repeat Robotics, Pololu) explicitly allowed as a non-plastic-restricted exemption for wheels/tires under most plastic-ant rulesets, offering better and more consistent grip than a printed tire.

entities.name: Small Flanged Ball Bearing (3-4mm bore)
entities.summary: A tiny flanged metal bearing used to support a plastic ant's weapon shaft, explicitly allowed as a metal exemption in every plastic-ant ruleset since bearings are functional hardware, not armor or weapon surface.

entities.name: Small-Diameter Steel Weapon Shaft
entities.summary: A short length of steel drill rod or precision shaft used to carry a plastic weapon disc/drum, exempt from the plastic-only rule as an 'axle' under SPARC-derived language as long as it does not itself act as an armor surface or weapon edge.

entities.name: M2/M3 Screws + Heat-Set Threaded Inserts
entities.summary: Small metal machine screws combined with brass heat-set threaded inserts melted into printed holes, the standard plastic-ant fastening method, explicitly allowed everywhere as long as screw heads on outer surfaces are countersunk or shrouded rather than left proud as de facto armor studs.

entities.name: Micro Slide/Toggle Power Switch
entities.summary: A small mechanical switch used as the required manual main power disconnect, mounted in a printed slot so it can be actuated without contacting moving parts, satisfying the SPARC-derived 15-second manual-disconnect rule.

entities.name: PLA+ (Modified PLA)
entities.summary: A modified PLA filament formulation marketed for improved impact resistance over standard PLA while keeping PLA's easy printability, one of the five materials SPARC and SCAR explicitly name as legal for plastic-ant chassis and weapons.

entities.name: PETG
entities.summary: A tougher, more impact-ductile filament than PLA, widely considered the best default choice for plastic-ant weapon discs/drums and load-bearing chassis members because it bends and absorbs energy rather than shattering.

entities.name: ABS
entities.summary: A strong, impact-resistant, comparatively low-density filament, one of the five universally-legal plastic-ant materials; harder to print reliably (needs an enclosure to prevent warping) but rewards the effort with a lighter, tougher part than PLA.

entities.name: TPU (Thermoplastic Polyurethane)
entities.summary: A rubber-like flexible printable filament popular in the wider combat-robot community for flexible armor panels and wheel tires because it bends and springs back instead of cracking — but it is NOT on the standard SPARC/SCAR approved-material list and is explicitly banned by name in SCAR's FAQ, making it a key org-to-org variance point in the plastic-ant class.

entities.name: Nylon (Printed)
entities.summary: A tough, wear-resistant, semi-flexible printable nylon filament that, like TPU, sits outside the base SPARC 4.4.1 approved list and is explicitly banned by name in SCAR's plastic ant FAQ, despite being a popular choice for gears and living-hinge parts in general 3D-printing use.

entities.name: Force Knight — Open-Source 1lb Plastic Antweight
entities.summary: A free, open-source 1lb plastic antweight design by community builder Michael K, published as downloadable STL files on Printables and described as intended for SCAR-legal component kits — a good example of the fully-open designs the plastic ant scene shares.

entities.name: CRNZ Antweight Combat Robot Kit
entities.summary: An open-source printable antweight chassis kit published by CombatRoboticsNZ on Thingiverse, designed to be extensible and modular so builders can swap weapon and drive modules without redesigning the whole robot.

entities.name: Legally Distinct — Open-Source 150g UK Drum Spinner Design
entities.summary: A free printable 150g UK-class antweight drum-spinner design by community builder Blessy (published on Thingiverse and documented on Hackaday.io), explicitly built as an homage/iteration on the established UK drum spinner 'Siren' — a clear, verified illustration of how the plastic scene iterates openly on successful designs.

entities.name: Siren (UK 150g Antweight / US Fairyweight)
entities.summary: A 150g UK-Antweight/US-Fairyweight drum-spinner combat robot by designer drcameron, published as free STL files on Thingiverse and Cults3D, well-known enough in the printable-antweight scene to have directly inspired the open-source 'Legally Distinct' drum spinner.

entities.name: Blunt Force Over Cutting
entities.summary: The plastic-ant design principle that, since no metal weapon edge is legal, weapons should be designed to transfer kinetic energy through mass and impact area (denting, cracking, flinging) rather than trying to cut or penetrate as a hardened steel blade would.

entities.name: COTS (Commercial Off-The-Shelf)
entities.summary: Parts bought ready-made rather than fabricated by the builder — motors, ESCs, receivers, bearings, and (per most plastic-ant FAQs) wheels/tires are explicitly allowed as COTS even though they aren't plastic, since the rule targets structural/armor/weapon plastic, not every component.

entities.name: Technical Inspection (Plastic-Only Check)
entities.summary: The pre-event safety/legality check where an event official visually inspects a plastic ant for compliance: verifying the chassis/armor/weapon are printed plastic, checking that any metal fasteners are countersunk/shrouded rather than proud, and looking for banned materials like TPU, nylon, or composite reinforcement layered into a printed part.

entities.name: Sacrificial Armor Panel
entities.summary: A deliberately weaker, easily-detachable printed panel placed over a robot's vulnerable areas so that a hit cracks/pops off the panel (a 5-minute reprint) instead of transmitting damage into the main chassis or electronics bay.

entities.name: Modular Bolt-On Section
entities.summary: A design pattern where the chassis is split into independently printed, bolt-together sections (e.g. separate front wedge, weapon pod, and drive base) so a single damaged section can be reprinted and swapped without remaking the whole robot.

entities.name: Printed-In Flexure
entities.summary: A thin, deliberately flexible section printed as part of a single larger piece (rather than a separate hinge with a pin) that acts as a spring or hinge — used in plastic ants for snap-fit panels, simple lifter linkages, and shock-absorbing mounts without adding a metal hinge part.

entities.name: Wall Count / Perimeters
entities.summary: The number of solid outer print loops (walls) surrounding a part's infill; combat-ready plastic ant parts typically use significantly more walls (5-8+) than a decorative print (2-3) because the solid perimeter, not the infill, carries most of an impact load.

entities.name: Infill Percentage (Combat Printing)
entities.summary: The proportion of a printed part's interior that is filled with a lattice pattern rather than left hollow; competitive plastic ant chassis parts commonly run 40-100% infill with a gyroid or cubic pattern, well above the 15-20% typical of non-structural prints, trading weight for toughness within the 454g budget.

entities.name: Layer Adhesion Anisotropy
entities.summary: The property that FDM-printed plastic is much stronger for forces applied parallel to its print layers than for forces trying to pull layers apart (perpendicular to them); the single most important physical fact plastic ant designers work around, driving choices about print orientation for weapons, wedges and shafts.

entities.name: Annealing (3D Print Post-Processing)
entities.summary: A post-print heat-treatment process (baking a printed part at a temperature below its melt point, sometimes packed in sand or salt to limit warping) that can meaningfully increase a part's layer strength and heat resistance; explicitly permitted post-processing under SCAR's plastic ant FAQ.

entities.name: Weight Budget
entities.summary: The practice of planning, before printing or buying anything, how the full 454g allowance will be split between armor/structure, weapon, drive, electronics and fasteners — critical in plastic ants because printed structure typically consumes over half the total weight, far more than in a metal antweight of the same class.

entities.name: Five-Minute Pit Repair
entities.summary: The plastic-ant repair philosophy of designing bolt-on, single-piece printed sub-assemblies so that a cracked wedge, wheel, or weapon can be swapped for a spare printed at home in under five minutes between matches, rather than requiring on-site fabrication or welding as a metal repair might.

entities.name: Robot Ruckus
entities.summary: A US SPARC-compliant combat robotics event run in conjunction with Maker Faire Orlando, popular with antweight and plastic-antweight builders. Insect weight classes (fairyweight/antweight/beetleweight) run double-elimination, while the larger 12lb/30lb/30lb-super-class divisions use a pools/Swiss fight format instead.

entities.name: SoCal Attack Robots (SCAR)
entities.summary: A Southern California combat robot organization/event series with one of the most detailed published Plastic Ant rulesets and FAQs in the US scene, explicitly naming approved filament brands and banning TPU/nylon.

entities.name: Bot Blast
entities.summary: An annual US insectweight-focused combat robotics event running a modified SPARC ruleset. Its main deviations from stock SPARC are a modified double-elimination format, a ban on autonomous robots, an immediate KO (at official discretion) for any robot with an exposed/damaged LiPo battery, and simplified judging criteria versus full SPARC judging.

entities.name: National Havoc Robot League (NHRL)
entities.summary: A major US combat robot league best known for its livestreamed 3lb (beetleweight) and 12/30lb events; NHRL itself is not the primary home of the 1lb plastic ant class (its own plastic-material class is Plastic Beetleweight), but many smaller 'NHRL-adjacent' local and remote-competition circuits run 1lb plastic ant undercards using a similar remote-competition/streamed format.

entities.name: FingerTech Robotics
entities.summary: A Canadian combat-robot parts supplier whose wheels, motors, and hubs are explicitly named as legal COTS options in plastic ant FAQs, making it one of the standard go-to sources for the non-plastic-exempt parts of a plastic ant build.

entities.name: Spinning Weapon Tip Speed
entities.summary: The standard combat-robotics formula for converting a spinning weapon's no-load RPM and diameter into tip speed in feet per second, taken verbatim from SPARC's Robot Construction Specifications (used to set/verify Sportsman-class and open-air tip-speed limits) and used informally by builders in every weight class, plastic ant included, to sanity-check a weapon design before it's built.

entities.name: 1104 brushless motor (weapon)
entities.summary: Tiny 11mm-diameter, 4mm-tall stator motor from the FPV whoop/toothpick world, used as an ultra-light vertical spinner or micro-drum motor on plastic antweights and fairyweights.

entities.name: 1106 brushless motor (weapon)
entities.summary: 11mm x 6mm stator motor, one step up from 1104 in stator height/torque, used for slightly heavier plastic-ant vertical spinners and paddle weapons.

entities.name: 1204 brushless motor (weapon)
entities.summary: 12mm-diameter, 4mm-tall stator motor, a common toothpick-drone motor repurposed as a plastic-ant or fairyweight vertical spinner/beater motor.

entities.name: 1306 brushless motor (weapon)
entities.summary: 13mm x 6mm stator motor originally built for FPV micro racing quads (2-3 inch props); a very common plastic-ant and light 1 lb weapon motor because of its wide KV range and cheap availability.

entities.name: 1404 brushless motor (weapon)
entities.summary: 14mm x 4mm stator motor, a step above 1306 in diameter (more torque, similar height); used on heavier plastic ants and light 1 lb spinners.

entities.name: 1408 brushless motor (weapon)
entities.summary: 14mm x 8mm stator motor, one of the most popular 'toothpick' drone sizes; a very common choice for 1 lb antweight vertical spinners, small drums, and light bars where a 1806 is too heavy.

entities.name: 1806 brushless motor (weapon)
entities.summary: 18mm x 6mm stator motor from the older 200-250 class mini-quad era; a long-running staple antweight weapon motor thanks to its 3mm shaft and 16x16mm M3 mount that make it easy to bolt straight to a hub or pulley.

entities.name: 2004 brushless motor (weapon)
entities.summary: 20mm x 4mm cinewhoop-derived stator, a lighter-weight alternative in the 20xx bracket for antweight builders who want a bit more diameter/torque than 1806 without the weight of a 2205+.

entities.name: 2205 brushless motor (weapon)
entities.summary: 22mm x 5mm stator, one of the definitive FPV racing-motor sizes and a very common 1 lb antweight vertical-disc/bar weapon motor because of its balance of torque, RPM range, and cheap availability.

entities.name: 2206 brushless motor (weapon)
entities.summary: 22mm x 6mm stator, a taller/torquier sibling of the 2205, popular in freestyle-quad builds and equally popular as an antweight bar or disc spinner motor.

entities.name: 2207 brushless motor (weapon)
entities.summary: 22mm x 7mm stator, one of the most common freestyle/racing FPV motor sizes and a direct antweight favorite; Repeat Robotics' antweight hubmotor is built on this stator size for plug-and-play direct-drive weapons.

entities.name: 2306 brushless motor (weapon)
entities.summary: 23mm x 6mm stator, the long-time standard 5-inch mini-quad motor size; used in antweights as a slightly larger-diameter alternative to the 22xx family for bar and drum spinners needing more torque.

entities.name: 2504 brushless motor (weapon)
entities.summary: 25mm x 4mm stator; a lighter member of the 25xx family used where extra diameter (torque) is wanted without jumping fully into 28xx weight, common on heavier 1 lb bar/drum builds pushing into light-beetle territory.

entities.name: 2508 brushless motor (weapon)
entities.summary: 25mm x 8mm stator, a tall/high-torque long-range and heavy-lift drone motor; in combat it is a low-KV, high-torque option for belt-reduced 1 lb drums and bars that need bite more than raw tip speed.

entities.name: 2806 brushless motor (weapon)
entities.summary: 28mm x 6mm stator, entry point of the 28xx family; used on heavy 1 lb builds and as a light-beetleweight crossover weapon motor, usually belt-driven to keep tip speed in range at low KV.

entities.name: 2812 brushless motor (weapon)
entities.summary: 28mm x 12mm stator, a very tall/torquey size from the heavy-lift/cinelifter drone world; occasionally used on the heaviest 1 lb builds or light beetles as a high-torque belt-driven weapon motor.

entities.name: 2814 brushless motor (weapon)
entities.summary: 28mm x 14mm stator, the classic heavy-lift/heavy-ant-beetle-crossover size; the Cobra 2814 in particular is a well-known belt-drive weapon motor used across heavy 1 lb and light beetleweight spinners.

entities.name: Repeat Robotics 2822 Weapon Motor
entities.summary: Purpose-built antweight weapon outrunner on a 28mm-diameter, 22mm-length can, sold specifically for direct-drive antweight spinners rather than repurposed from a drone; widely regarded as one of the most durable off-the-shelf antweight weapon motors.

entities.name: Repeat Robotics 2207 Battle Ready Hubmotor
entities.summary: A 2207-stator combat hubmotor sold as a complete direct-drive weapon solution for antweights: the weapon hub/disc bolts straight to the motor bell, eliminating a separate shaft-and-bearing weapon assembly.

entities.name: Repeat Robotics Scalar Antweight Weapon Motor (2305)
entities.summary: A 23mm-stator-class purpose-built antweight weapon motor with an oversized ~28.2mm outer bell for extra rotor mass/flywheel effect relative to its stator size.

entities.name: RDY-5022 Antweight Hubmotor
entities.summary: Just 'Cuz Robotics antweight direct-drive hubmotor, offered in 1100kv and 1700kv windings, sized for antweight vertical spinners at typical 3-4S antweight voltages.

entities.name: RDY-5536 Beetleweight Hubmotor
entities.summary: Just 'Cuz Robotics beetleweight-class direct-drive hubmotor, offered in 900kv and 1200kv windings; relevant to antweights mainly as the upper end of the size ladder / heavy-ant crossover reference point.

entities.name: JCR-4935 Horizontal Spinner Motor
entities.summary: Just 'Cuz Robotics 1000kv motor specifically marketed for horizontal spinners (bars/blades spun about a vertical-ish or horizontal axis with high aerodynamic drag), where a lower KV is used to keep current sane against drag.

entities.name: BadAss 23-series 2315 Weapon Motor
entities.summary: A 23mm-diameter, 15mm-length belt-drive weapon motor at 1480kv, cited as a common antweight/heavy-ant belt-drive option that trades some direct-drive simplicity for a taller, torquier stator than typical 23xx drone motors.

entities.name: Turbo 2830 Weapon Motor
entities.summary: A 28mm-diameter, 30mm-length belt-drive weapon motor at 1300kv; one of the largest commonly cited motors used at the antweight/beetleweight belt-drive crossover for high-torque drums and bars.

entities.name: Required motor KV from target tip speed and battery voltage
entities.summary: Back-solves the motor KV (or KV x gear-ratio) needed to hit a target tip speed on a given battery voltage, the single most common weapon-motor sizing question in the hobby.

entities.name: Rotational kinetic energy stored in a spinning weapon
entities.summary: Computes the joules of kinetic energy stored in a weapon flywheel from its moment of inertia and angular velocity -- the number that actually predicts damage potential, not RPM alone.

entities.name: Weapon spin-up time estimate from torque and MOI
entities.summary: Estimates the time to bring a weapon from rest to full speed given the weapon's moment of inertia and the motor's average available accelerating torque over that speed range -- the calculation that explains why an underpowered motor loses matches before the fight even starts.

entities.name: Weapon motor peak and steady electrical power draw
entities.summary: Estimates electrical power draw during weapon spin-up (near stall) versus steady-state windmilling, used to size battery C-rating and ESC current headroom.

entities.name: RPM to angular velocity (rad/s) conversion
entities.summary: Simple unit conversion used throughout weapon-motor sizing math to move between RPM (what motor/ESC specs use) and rad/s (what physics formulas for torque, power and kinetic energy need).

entities.name: KV (motor velocity constant)
entities.summary: The unloaded RPM a brushless motor spins per volt applied, in RPM/V. Determines top speed for a given voltage, but says nothing about torque or power by itself -- a motor's stator size and winding resistance matter just as much.

entities.name: Stator volume (diameter x height)
entities.summary: The product of a brushless motor's stator diameter and stator height/stack length, encoded directly in FPV motor names (e.g. '2207' = 22mm diameter x 7mm height). Stator volume is the single best predictor of how much torque and continuous power a motor can produce, because it sets how much copper and iron can be packed in to carry current and hold magnetic flux without saturating.

entities.name: Back-EMF (counter-electromotive force)
entities.summary: The voltage a spinning motor generates that opposes the applied drive voltage, proportional to RPM and inversely proportional to KV (Back-EMF volts = RPM / KV). As a weapon motor spins up, rising back-EMF is what makes available current -- and therefore torque -- fall off as speed increases, producing the classic linear torque-speed line.

entities.name: Outrunner vs inrunner
entities.summary: Outrunner motors spin the outer magnet-lined bell/can around a fixed inner stator (the common FPV/drone layout); inrunner motors spin a small magnet rotor inside a fixed outer stator can. Outrunners dominate weapon-motor use because their larger effective rotor radius gives more torque per amp and the bell itself doubles as a flywheel/weapon-mounting surface.

entities.name: Dead shaft (weapon mounting)
entities.summary: A weapon-mounting scheme where the shaft itself does not rotate -- it is bolted rigidly to the frame -- while the weapon blade/hub and its pulley (bolted together) spin freely around the fixed shaft on bearings pressed into the hub.

entities.name: Bite (weapon engagement depth)
entities.summary: How deeply a spinning weapon's tooth/edge engages an opponent's armor per revolution before sliding off -- determined by weapon RPM relative to the combined driving speed of both robots, not by tip speed or KE alone. Lower weapon RPM (for the same tip speed, i.e. bigger diameter/lower KV) generally gives more bite because the tooth has more time to dig in per revolution.

entities.name: Demagnetization (weapon motor failure)
entities.summary: Permanent partial loss of magnetic strength in a motor's rotor magnets, caused by driving current far beyond the motor's rated stall current (common during a hard weapon-vs-weapon or weapon-vs-wall impact stall) or by sustained overheating past the magnet's Curie-adjacent temperature limit. A demagnetized motor permanently loses torque and top KV-equivalent speed even after the fault current stops.

entities.name: Fairyweight (150g)
entities.summary: The smallest weight class in common use, capped at 150 grams (about 0.33 lb). In the US/SPARC world it is called Fairyweight; confusingly, this exact 150g limit is what British builders call 'Antweight', which is far lighter than the US 1lb antweight. It is a popular entry point because parts are cheap and damage is minimal.

entities.name: Antweight (1 lb)
entities.summary: The classic North American entry class, capped at 1 lb (454 g). It is the most-run class at US and Canadian events (SPARC, RoboGames, Motorama, Robot Ruckus, Bot Blast) and is roughly three times heavier than the UK 'Antweight' (150 g), a naming collision that trips up new builders reading rules from the wrong region.

entities.name: Beetleweight (3 lb)
entities.summary: A 3 lb (1.36 kg) class, the second most popular class in the US after antweight, and one of NHRL's three official divisions. It allows meaningfully more powerful weapons and drivetrains than antweight while still being affordable and easy to transport.

entities.name: Plastic Beetleweight
entities.summary: The 3 lb equivalent of plastic antweight: robots must be built almost entirely from approved 3D-printable plastics rather than metal. Less common than plastic antweight but growing at the same regional US events that run plastic-only brackets.

entities.name: Hobbyweight (12 lb)
entities.summary: A 12 lb (5.44 kg) middle-tier class, one of NHRL's three flagship divisions and a common SPARC class. It's a step up in cost and danger from beetleweight, generally viewed as an intermediate builder's class.

entities.name: Featherweight (30 lb)
entities.summary: A 30 lb (13.6 kg) class, NHRL's largest flagship division and a long-standing SPARC/RoboGames class. Featherweight fights are visibly more destructive than smaller classes and require more serious safety gear and containment.

entities.name: Lightweight (60 lb)
entities.summary: A 60 lb (27.2 kg) class run mainly by SPARC and RoboGames. It sits between the popular small hobby classes and the TV-scale heavyweights, requiring real machine-shop fabrication and industrial-grade components.

entities.name: Middleweight (120 lb)
entities.summary: A 120 lb (54.4 kg) class run by SPARC and RoboGames, sitting just below the TV-scale heavyweight class. Robots at this size need hydraulic/pneumatic or large brushless weapon systems and significant safety infrastructure.

entities.name: Heavyweight (220-250 lb)
entities.summary: The top-tier 'TV weight' class. BattleBots' modern single division caps at 250 lb (113 kg) ready-to-fight, while SPARC's traditional heavyweight class is 220 lb (100 kg); RoboGames also runs a 250 lb class plus a heavier walking-bonus tier. These robots require professional-grade fabrication, hydraulics/large brushless weapons, and are only run at events with heavy-duty arenas.

entities.name: SPARC (Standardized Procedures for the Advancement of Robotic Combat)
entities.summary: SPARC is the dominant unified US/international rule set for hobby-scale combat robotics. A single 'SPARC-legal' build is accepted at essentially every SPARC-compliant event worldwide, covering weight classes from fairyweight (150g) up to heavyweight (220 lb), plastic-class material rules, weight bonuses for walkers/shufflers, multibot/clusterbot rules, and standardized safety requirements.

entities.name: NHRL Open Rules (National Havoc Robot League)
entities.summary: NHRL runs the largest recurring US combat robotics series (Franklin, MA) across exactly three weight classes: 3lb (beetleweight), 12lb (hobbyweight), and 30lb (featherweight). It uses a qualifying-then-bracket tournament format, mandatory weapon locks and radio failsafe testing, and pays cash prizes, which distinguishes it from most hobbyist-only events.

entities.name: RoboGames Combat Robot Rules
